main_point: The U.S. Supreme Court is hearing a landmark case where entertainment companies seek to hold P2P software makers liable for copyright infringement, a ruling that could overturn the 1984 Betamax precedent and determine the future legality of peer-to-peer technology in the U.S.

actors.canonical_name: Sony Corp. v. Universal City Studios

statements.text: On March 29, the U.S. Supreme Court listened to oral arguments in the MGM v. Grokster case. In this lawsuit, 28 entertainment companies sued peer-to-peer software makers, asking the court to make them legally liable for copyright infringement. The case aims to reverse the 1984 Betamax precedent. That earlier ruling had shielded technology distributors. This decision will decide whether peer-to-peer networks are legal in the United States.
statements.text_short: A landmark case is before the U.S. Supreme Court. Entertainment firms want to make P2P software makers responsible for copyright infringement. This decision might change the 1984 Betamax precedent. It could also decide if peer-to-peer technology is legal in the U.S.

statements.text: A recent survey by the Pew Internet & American Life Project reveals that 49% of all Americans and 53% of internet users believe that owners of file-sharing networks should be held legally responsible for the piracy of music and movie files. This public opinion data underscores a significant societal demand for stricter liability regarding digital content distribution, contrasting with the legal protections previously afforded to technology companies.
statements.text_short: A recent survey by the Pew Internet & American Life Project reveals that 49% of all Americans and 53% of internet users believe that owners of file-sharing networks should be held legally responsible for the piracy of music and movie files.

statements.text: The outcome of the MGM v. Grokster case will either affirm the 1984 Betamax precedent or overturn it, representing a pivotal moment for the U.S. technology sector. This legal decision carries billions of dollars in future revenues at stake, as it determines whether modern peer-to-peer technology will be protected under the same legal framework that originally enabled the home video market.
statements.text_short: The MGM v. Grokster ruling will either uphold the 1984 Betamax decision or reverse it. This result is a critical turning point for the U.S. technology industry, as billions of dollars in future income depend on the outcome.
